title: Chapter 60 — The Line
paragraphs: With reference to the whaling scene soon to be described, as well as for the better understanding of all similar scenes presented elsewhere, I must speak here of the magical, sometimes horrible whale-line.

The line originally used in the fishery was of the best hemp, slightly coated with tar — not soaked in it, as with ordinary ropes. For while tar, as ordinarily used, makes hemp more pliable for the ropemaker and also makes the rope itself more convenient for common ship use, not only would the usual amount stiffen the whale-line too much for the close coiling it must undergo, but tar in general tends to rot rather than preserve the line. Thus the original line was merely touched with tar.

In recent years, Manila rope has in the American fishery almost entirely replaced hemp as a material for whale-lines. Though not as durable as hemp, it is stronger and far more soft and elastic. And I will add — since there is an aesthetics in all things — it is much more handsome and attractive in the boat than hemp. Hemp is a dusky, dark fellow, a sort of Indian. But Manila is like a golden-haired beauty to look at.

The whale-line is only two-thirds of an inch thick. At first sight you would not think it so strong as it really is. By experiment, each of its fifty-one yarns will suspend a weight of one hundred and twenty pounds, so that the whole rope will bear a strain of nearly three tons. In length, the common sperm whale-line measures something over two hundred fathoms. Toward the stern of the boat it is spirally coiled away in the tub — not like the pipe of a still, but in such a way that any free end can be pulled out without disturbing the rest of the coil. This way, the line is kept ready for instant use.

In English boats, two tubs are used instead of one, with the same line continuously coiled in both tubs. There is some advantage in this, because the twin tubs, being smaller, fit more easily into the boat and put less strain on it. Whereas the American tub, nearly three feet in diameter and of proportionate depth, makes rather bulky freight for a craft whose planks are but half an inch thick. For the bottom of the whale-boat is like thin ice — it will hold up a decent enough weight, but you don't want to be standing on it too long.

Both ends of the line are exposed. The lower end terminates in a loop coming up from the bottom against the side of the tub and hanging over its edge, completely free. This arrangement of the lower end is necessary for two reasons. First: to allow an additional line from a neighboring boat to be attached to it, in case the struck whale should dive so deep as to threaten to carry off the entire original line. In these instances, the line of a neighboring boat is fastened to the end of the line already attached to the whale. Second: this arrangement is necessary because of a universal law of the whale fishery — that no line can be used in active service until it has been rearranged and re-coiled from one tub into another.

Before lowering the boat for the chase, the upper end of the line is taken aft from the tub and passed around the loggerhead, then carried forward the entire length of the boat, resting crosswise upon the handle of every man's oar so that it jogs against his wrist in rowing. It also passes between the men as they alternately sit at opposite gunwales, to the grooved fittings in the extreme pointed prow of the boat, where a wooden pin the size of a common quill directs it outward. From there it hangs in a short arc over the bow, and is free to fly off at the darting of the harpoon.

Thus the whale-line wraps the whole boat in its complicated coils, twisting and writhing around it in almost every direction. All the oarsmen are caught up in its dangerous tangles, so that to the timid eye of the landsman, they look like Indian jugglers with the deadliest snakes playfully draped around their limbs. Nor can any mortal man, sitting amid those hempen intricacies for the first time, and straining his utmost at the oar, easily forget that at any unknown instant the harpoon may be thrown, and all these horrible coils will go spinning through him and snatch him into the deep.

Perhaps a very little thought will now help you understand those repeated whaling disasters — some few of which are casually recorded — of this man or that man being pulled out of the boat by the line and lost. For when the line is running out, to be seated in the boat is like being seated in the midst of the whizzing parts of a steam-engine running at full power, when every flying beam and shaft and wheel is grazing you. It is worse, for you cannot sit still in the heart of these dangers, because the boat itself is always rocking. Only by the most careful attention to the direction of the spinning line, and by occasionally jerking the oar, can you hope to escape instant destruction.

Again: as the deep calm that only apparently precedes and foretells the storm is perhaps more dreadful than the storm itself — for the calm is merely the storm's wrapper and envelope, containing it within itself, as the seemingly harmless rifle holds the fatal powder, the ball, and the explosion — so the graceful stillness of the line, as it silently coils around the oarsmen before being brought into actual play, carries more true terror than any other aspect of this dangerous business. But why say more? All men live surrounded by invisible whale-lines. All are born with halters round their necks. And a swift, sudden turn of death may come upon any of us at any moment. Only the difference is this: the whale-line makes the danger visible.
